309.title: The teacher
309.hook: in Tibetan practice the teacher is central; students are told to check a teacher for years first
309.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism students usually study with a lama who gives teachings, reading transmissions and empowerments; many teachers advise students to observe a teacher for a long time before committing to one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four thoughts that turn the mind, and your line, turn the mind. When an old groove pulled at you, did you pause and choose? Day three hundred nine.

You wouldn't hire a contractor without checking references. You'd read the reviews before choosing a dentist. And yet people sometimes hand their whole inner life to a charismatic stranger after one inspiring weekend. Here's what's surprising. The tradition that puts the teacher at the very center of the path, Tibetan Buddhism, is also the one that tells students, loudly and in writing: slow down. Check first. Some texts say to take years. Today: the lama, and how to look at one.
screen: `REFERENCES FOR A CONTRACTOR.` → `ONE WEEKEND, A WHOLE LIFE.` → `SLOW DOWN. CHECK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Lama is the Tibetan word for the Sanskrit guru. Guru literally means heavy: someone of weight, whose words land. Tibetans give lama their own warm explanations too; a common one says it means none higher. Why is the teacher so central here? Because many Vajrayana practices are passed from person to person. A teacher reads the text aloud so the student receives it, gives permission for a practice, and shows how it's done, the way a music teacher shows you how to hold the bow. You can read about the violin forever. At some point, someone has to hear you play. But the same tradition insists on caution. A text called the Fifty Verses on the Guru tells teacher and student to examine each other first, and Tibetan teachers often say this can take as long as twelve years. The Dalai Lama has said many times that students should scrutinize a teacher carefully, and that no one should follow an instruction that goes against the teaching or against basic ethics. Classic lists describe a good teacher as disciplined, calm, learned, kind, patient, and honest about what they don't know. And there are warning signs anyone can see: pressure, secrecy, money that's never explained, being cut off from friends, behavior that breaks the very precepts being taught. Sadly, recent decades have shown why this matters: some communities have been hurt by teachers who abused their trust, and many Tibetan teachers have said such harm must be named. The heart of it is simple. Trust is given slowly, and it stays open to question. Check the teacher.
screen: `LAMA — GURU, ONE OF WEIGHT.` · `PASSED FROM PERSON TO PERSON.` · `EXAMINE EACH OTHER, FOR YEARS.` · `SIGNS OF A GOOD TEACHER, AND WARNINGS.` · then, large: `CHECK THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, think of anyone who has taught you something that mattered: a coach, a grandparent, a boss, a teacher in any field. What made them trustworthy? Maybe they admitted mistakes. Maybe they never asked for more than they gave. Silently name two or three of those qualities. Then let the list go, and sit with the breath, noticing that you, too, get to be careful about whom you trust. The bell holds the time.
Lama. The Tibetan word for guru, a teacher of weight: central to the path, and to be examined carefully first.
Your line: check the teacher. Today, write down the qualities you named, so you have them the next time someone asks for your trust. Day three hundred nine.

options: obey: the teacher is central.

fork.reveal: the tradition that makes the teacher central also says to examine a teacher carefully and not follow instructions against basic ethics.

310.title: Tonglen
310.hook: sending and taking: breathe in another's pain, breathe out relief
310.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists practice tonglen as part of mind training, usually beginning with their own suffering and widening to others, breathing in suffering and breathing out relief; it's also practiced at the bedside of the sick and dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lama, and your line, check the teacher. Did you write down what makes someone worth trusting? Day three hundred ten.

You've probably heard it in a yoga class or a stress app. Breathe in calm. Breathe out tension. Take in the good, push out the bad. It makes sense: that's what every instinct in the body wants to do. Now imagine a practice that turns it exactly around. Breathe in someone else's pain. Breathe out relief, toward them. It sounds backward, maybe even a little dangerous. Tibetan teachers have taught it for nearly a thousand years. Today: tonglen.
screen: `BREATHE IN CALM, OUT TENSION.` → `NOW TURN IT AROUND.` → `IN: PAIN. OUT: RELIEF.`

segments.voice: Tonglen is two Tibetan words. Tong: sending, giving away. Len: taking, receiving. It comes from the mind-training teachings the Indian master Atisha brought to Tibet in the eleventh century, and one of their short sayings puts it simply: practice sending and taking in turn, and let the two ride the breath. Here's how teachers usually describe it. As you breathe in, you picture taking in someone's suffering, often imagined as dark, heavy smoke. As you breathe out, you send them relief: light, coolness, space, whatever would help. Most teachers say to start where it's easiest. First your own pain, just as it is. Then someone you love who's hurting. Then a stranger who feels the same thing. Then everyone who feels it tonight. Why would anyone want to breathe in pain? Because, the teachers say, our habit of shoving pain away and grabbing comfort is exactly what keeps the heart small and scared. Tonglen reverses the habit. People who practice it often report that pain frightens them less, not more. Does it take the pain away from the other person? Teachers answer in different ways. Many say its main work is on the practitioner's own heart; many Tibetans also hold that it can truly benefit others. It's karuna, compassion, one of the four rooms from the start of this camp, given a rhythm. And there's a gentle rule. If it overwhelms you, go back to your own pain, or simply rest. Nobody is asked to carry the whole world in one breath. Take in, send out.
screen: `TONG, SENDING. LEN, TAKING.` · `IN: DARK SMOKE. OUT: LIGHT.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN WIDEN.` · `REVERSING THE HABIT.` · then, large: `TAKE IN, SEND OUT.`

segments.voice: Let's try a gentle round. Start with something you feel right now, a tiredness, a worry. Breathe it in, as if making room for it, not fighting it. Breathe out ease, toward yourself. After a few breaths, think of one person who is struggling. Breathe in their heaviness, and breathe out something that might help them. If it ever feels like too much, go back to your own breath and rest. The bell holds the time.
Tonglen. Sending and taking: breathing in another's pain and breathing out relief, a compassion practice that rides the breath.
Your line: take in, send out. Today, when you see someone struggling, a stranger in traffic, a tired cashier, take one quiet breath for them. Day three hundred ten.

sources.ref: Chekawa Yeshe Dorje, Seven-Point Mind Training (the slogan on sending and taking riding the breath)

311.title: Mind training
311.hook: the slogans of Atisha's tradition, such as "drive all blames into one"
311.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists study the lojong slogans, often in Geshe Chekawa's Seven-Point Mind Training, memorize them, and bring one slogan at a time into daily situations, especially difficult ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tonglen, and your line, take in, send out. Did you take one quiet breath for someone who was struggling? Day three hundred eleven.

Look around a few kitchens and you'll find them. A sticky note on the mirror. A magnet on the fridge. A line written on the inside of a wrist. Short sentences people keep where they'll bump into them, because a long book won't be there at the moment you snap at your kid or your coworker. Tibetan Buddhists have a set of lines like that, about fifty-nine of them, and they're nearly a thousand years old. One of them sounds almost rude at first: drive all blames into one. Today: mind training.
screen: `A STICKY NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A LINE FOR THE HARD MOMENT.` → `DRIVE ALL BLAMES INTO ONE.`

segments.voice: Lojong. Lo is mind; jong means training, or cleaning up. The teachings trace to Atisha, the Bengali master who came to Tibet in the eleventh century. There's a story people tell about him: he brought along a cranky servant who argued with everything, because he needed someone to practice patience on. When he heard how kind the Tibetans were, he wondered if he'd still need the servant. A century later a teacher named Geshe Chekawa gathered the teachings into short slogans, meant to be memorized and carried. Some are gentle. Be grateful to everyone. Always keep a joyful mind. Some are sharp. Don't wait in ambush. Don't talk about other people's faults. And then: drive all blames into one. It does not mean blame yourself for everything. Tibetan teachers are clear about that. The one is self-cherishing: the habit that puts me at the center of every story and then feels outraged when the world doesn't cooperate. So when something goes wrong, instead of scanning the room for someone to blame, you look at the grasping in your own reaction. That's where the heat is coming from, and it's the one thing you can actually work with. It doesn't excuse harm, and it doesn't mean staying where you're hurt. It means your own mind is the training ground. Be grateful to everyone fits the same way: the difficult coworker is Atisha's cranky servant, giving you something to practice on. Teachers suggest carrying just one slogan at a time, and letting it meet the day. One slogan.
screen: `LO, MIND. JONG, TRAINING.` · `ATISHA AND THE CRANKY SERVANT.` · `THE ONE IS SELF-CHERISHING.` · `YOUR MIND, THE TRAINING GROUND.` · then, large: `ONE SLOGAN.`

segments.voice: For this sit, choose one slogan to carry. Drive all blames into one. Be grateful to everyone. Always keep a joyful mind. Pick the one that pinches a little. Say it silently once, then sit with the breath. When a thought or an irritation comes, see if the slogan has anything to say to it. You don't need to force an answer. Just let the line and the moment meet. The bell holds the time.
Lojong. Mind training: short slogans from Atisha's tradition, carried into the day so the hard moments become the practice.
Your line: one slogan. Write the one you chose somewhere you'll bump into it today, and when you do, let it meet whatever's happening. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: Bodhicitta
312.hook: the mind that wants to wake up for the sake of all beings
312.howItsDone: Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhists generate bodhicitta at the start of practice, often reciting a short refuge and bodhicitta verse, and end by dedicating the merit to all beings; many also take formal bodhisattva vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lojong, and your line, one slogan. Did you bump into the line you chose, and did it have anything to say? Day three hundred twelve.

Every flight, the same speech. If the cabin loses pressure, masks will drop. Put on your own mask first, then help the person next to you. It sounds selfish for about one second, until you realize the point: you can't help anyone if you've passed out. Now imagine that someone put on their mask only because of the person next to them. And the row behind. And every passenger on every plane. That's the reason Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhists give for practicing at all. Today: bodhicitta.
screen: `PUT ON YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.` → `SO YOU CAN HELP THE NEXT PERSON.` → `AND EVERY PASSENGER, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Bodhicitta. Bodhi, awakening, the word you met under the tree. Citta, mind or heart. The awakening mind: the wish to wake up not just for yourself, but so you can help every being do the same. In Tibetan practice it's the engine of everything. The four thoughts turn the mind; bodhicitta tells it where to go. The great teacher of bodhicitta is Shantideva, an Indian monk of the eighth century. A story people tell: at the great monastery of Nalanda, the other monks thought he was lazy, good only for eating, sleeping and strolling around. To embarrass him, they asked him to teach in public. He sat down and recited a whole long poem, The Way of the Bodhisattva, and the monks were stunned. In it he makes a simple distinction. There's wanting to go on a journey, and there's actually setting out. Bodhicitta has both: the wish, and then the steps, in giving, patience, effort and the rest. And the poem ends with a vow people still say today, in paraphrase: for as long as space remains and beings remain, may I remain too, to ease the world's suffering. Where traditions differ, it's worth saying clearly. In the Theravada, the elders honor the bodhisattva's road as the Buddha's own long path through the Jataka lives, and most practitioners aim at awakening as an arahant. In the Mahayana and the Vajrayana, bodhicitta is placed at the start of the path for everyone. That's why Tibetan practices end by dedicating whatever good was done to all beings. Not for me. For all of us.
screen: `BODHI, AWAKENING. CITTA, MIND.` · `SHANTIDEVA AT NALANDA.` · `WANTING TO GO, THEN SETTING OUT.` · `AS LONG AS SPACE REMAINS.` · then, large: `FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: For this sit, try dedicating it. Before the bell, silently set the intention: whatever good comes from this sit, may it help someone. Then widen it: may it help everyone. You don't need to feel anything special. Then just sit with the breath, as usual. When the sit ends, if you'd like, give it away once more: whatever good came from this, for all of us. The bell holds the time.
Bodhicitta. The awakening mind: the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings, and the steps that follow the wish.
Your line: for all of us. Today, before one ordinary task, a meeting, a commute, the dishes, quietly dedicate it to everyone it might touch. Day three hundred twelve.

trapdoor: what you thought: being a nice person.
what it means: the wish to wake up fully for the sake of all beings, and the practice that follows.

313.title: Tara
313.hook: Green Tara, the bodhisattva who acts swiftly to protect
313.howItsDone: Many Tibetan Buddhists recite Tara's mantra and the Praise to the Twenty-One Taras daily, turn to Green Tara in times of danger or fear, and keep her image on household shrines.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bodhicitta, and your line, for all of us. Did you dedicate one ordinary task to everyone it might touch? Day three hundred thirteen.

When you're scared, really scared, a car sliding on ice, a child with a fever at three in the morning, you don't want a long lecture. You want someone who comes quickly. Now picture a painting on a Tibetan wall: a woman seated on a lotus, her body green like young leaves. Her left leg is folded in meditation. But her right leg is stretched out, foot already stepping down off the seat, as if she's heard you and is on her way. Today: Tara.
screen: `A CAR ON ICE. A FEVER AT 3 A.M.` → `A WOMAN ON A LOTUS, GREEN.` → `ONE FOOT STEPPING DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tara, whom Tibetans call Dolma, is one of the best-loved figures in Tibetan Buddhism. Her name has two meanings in Sanskrit: star, the light you steer by, and she who carries across, like a ferry over a river. A well-known story says she was born from compassion itself. Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva you met in the Heart Sutra and in the six syllables, looked at the suffering of the world and wept. Where a tear fell, a lotus grew, and from the lotus rose Tara. Another story, told in a later Tibetan history, is about a princess named Wisdom Moon who practiced so deeply that monks advised her to pray for rebirth as a man, to reach awakening. She answered that in the deepest sense there is no man or woman to cling to, and she vowed to keep working for beings in a woman's form until all are free. There are many Taras. White Tara is linked with long life and healing. Green Tara is swift, active protection, and that stepping-down foot is the whole point: compassion that doesn't wait. A famous hymn praises twenty-one forms of Tara, and many Tibetans chant it every morning. Tradition says she protects from eight fears: lions, elephants, fire, snakes, thieves, prison, floods and demons. Later teachers read those inwardly too: pride, confusion, anger, envy, wrong views, greed, clinging and doubt. Many Tibetans turn to her in any trouble, big or small, and trust her the way you trust someone who picks up on the first ring. She comes quickly.
screen: `TARA — STAR, AND THE ONE WHO FERRIES.` · `BORN FROM A TEAR OF COMPASSION.` · `THE PRINCESS WISDOM MOON.` · `EIGHT FEARS, OUTSIDE AND IN.` · then, large: `SHE COMES QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: For this sit, picture a quick, kind helper. It can be Green Tara, green as new leaves, one foot stepping toward you. Or it can be someone from your own life who always came when you called. Let their presence settle next to you. Then turn it around: imagine being that quick, kind helper for someone else today. Let the picture fade, and rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Tara. The star, the one who ferries across: in Tibetan Buddhism, the bodhisattva of swift compassion, one foot already stepping down.
Your line: she comes quickly. Today, when someone asks for help, even something small, answer a little faster than you normally would. Day three hundred thirteen.

pairs: star; the one who ferries across

it shows compassion that doesn't wait: she's already on her way.

fork.reveal: in the story she vows to keep working for beings in a woman's form until all are free, and becomes Tara.

original.note: Sanskrit tārā: star, and she who carries across. Tibetan: Dolma (sgrol ma), 'she who frees'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess who grants wishes.
what it means: a bodhisattva of swift compassion who protects from fear and ferries beings across.

314.title: The sand mandala
314.hook: monks build a mandala of colored sand for days, then sweep it into a river
314.howItsDone: Tibetan monks construct sand mandalas for particular rituals and, increasingly, for public events; when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala, give some sand to those present and pour the rest into flowing water.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara, and your line, she comes quickly. When someone asked for help, did you answer a little faster? Day three hundred fourteen.

Imagine a museum lobby, or a college gym. A small group of Tibetan monks has set up a low table. For days, sometimes weeks, they lean over it, tapping thin metal funnels, and grains of colored sand trickle out a few at a time. People come back every afternoon to watch it grow: palaces, gates, lotus petals, sharp lines finer than a pencil could draw. Then, on the last day, with everyone watching, a monk draws a line straight through the middle. Today: the sand mandala.
screen: `A LOW TABLE, A FEW MONKS.` → `SAND, A FEW GRAINS AT A TIME.` → `A LINE THROUGH THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Mandala is Sanskrit for circle. In Tibetan practice it's more than a pattern: it's a map of an awakened world, often the palace of a Buddha or deity seen from above, with four gates facing the four directions, walls in bright colors, and the deity at the very center. People meditate on it, and some rituals take place in relation to it. Mandalas can be painted, or built in three dimensions, or pictured in the mind. The sand mandala is the most delicate. Monks use a narrow metal funnel with ridges along its side; rubbing a rod across the ridges makes it vibrate, and the sand falls grain by grain. Teams work from the center outward, following exact measurements handed down in the texts. It can take days, or weeks. And then the ending, which is the part people remember. When the rituals are complete, the lines are cut through and the sand is swept toward the center into one gray-brown pile. Some is given to the people watching, as a blessing. The rest is carried to a river or stream and poured into the water, so the blessing flows out into the world, like the wind through the prayer flags. Why build something so beautiful and then destroy it? Tibetan teachers give more than one reason. The sweeping teaches impermanence, which you've met since the first sight of an old man. It teaches letting go of what we make. And it shows that the blessing was never meant to stay in one room. The work was real. The beauty was real. And it's swept away.
screen: `MANDALA — CIRCLE, A MAP OF AWAKENING.` · `SAND, GRAIN BY GRAIN, FOR DAYS.` · `SWEPT TO THE CENTER.` · `POURED INTO THE RIVER.` · then, large: `SWEPT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, make something small. Arrange a few objects on a table into a pattern: coins, pens, leaves, whatever's near. Take care with it, just for a moment. Look at it. Then gently mix it up, and let it go. Notice any small tug of not wanting to. Then sit, and let each breath arrive and pass, built and swept away. The bell holds the time.
Mandala. A circle: a map of an awakened world, built in sand with great care, then swept away and poured into the river.
Your line: swept away. Today, do one thing well that won't last, a meal, a clean counter, a kind message, and let it go without needing it to stay. Day three hundred fourteen.

mandala means circle

fork.reveal: it's swept to the center; some sand is given away and the rest goes into flowing water, a teaching on impermanence and letting go.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty circular pattern.
what it means: a map of an awakened world, built with care and then swept away.

315.title: Four schools
315.hook: Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug: later years explain each, never ranked
315.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists usually practice within one of the four schools, Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya or Gelug, through a particular teacher and monastery, and many also receive teachings from other schools in the nonsectarian spirit of the Rime movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sand mandala, and your line, swept away. Did you do one thing well and let it go without needing it to last? Day three hundred fifteen, the end of the week.

Some of the great rivers of Asia begin on the Tibetan plateau. The same snow, the same high ground, and then they run off in different directions, through different valleys, feeding different fields, each one a whole river. Tibetan Buddhism is a little like that. Walk into four monasteries and you may hear four styles of chanting, see four different hats, and meet four lines of teachers going back centuries. Same high ground. Different valleys. Today: the four schools, just their names and a first glance.
screen: `RIVERS FROM THE SAME HIGH GROUND.` → `DIFFERENT VALLEYS, WHOLE RIVERS.` → `FOUR MONASTERIES, FOUR STYLES.`

segments.voice: Nyingma means the old ones. It carries the earliest translations, from the time of Padmasambhava in the eighth century, and it's known for a teaching called dzogchen, the great perfection. Kagyu means the lineage of the spoken word. It runs from Marpa the translator to his student Milarepa, the poet who lived in mountain caves, to Gampopa, whose book gave you the four thoughts. Its best-known teaching is mahamudra, the great seal. Sakya is named for the gray earth where its first monastery was built in the eleventh century, and a single family has guided it for generations. Its central teaching is called the path and its fruit. Gelug means the virtuous ones. It was founded by the scholar Tsongkhapa around six hundred years ago, with a strong emphasis on monastic discipline, study and debate; the Dalai Lamas come from this school. Here's what they share. The same monastic code. The Mahayana heart of bodhicitta. The Vajrayana tools of mantra and visualization. The four differ in lineage, in emphasis, in which texts come first. In the nineteenth century a movement called Rime, meaning without sides, urged Tibetans to learn from all of them. And alongside the four lives Bön, Tibet's own old religious tradition, with lineages of its own. Later years will open each school properly. For now, the names, and no ranking. Now look back at the week. Check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. And today: four streams.

segments.voice: Before the sit, name the four slowly, one per breath. Nyingma. Kagyu. Sakya. Gelug. Picture four rivers leaving the same snowfield. Then let the names go, and sit with the breath, which is the same breath whichever valley you're in. When the mind wanders, come back to the high, quiet ground. The bell holds the time.
Four schools. Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug: four lineages of Tibetan Buddhism, sharing one heart, each a whole way.
Your line: four streams. Today, when you meet people who do the same thing differently, notice what they share before you notice what they don't. Day three hundred fifteen.
